snippet.title: How Learning To Code Changed My Life (and things it taught me)
snippet.description:
I started to learn to code when I was 20 years old, and within a year, I was already working as a software engineer at one of the top tech companies, and the whole experience, completely changed my life for the better. 

Let’s back up - I’m originally from Belarus, where I spent the majority of my life. When I was 17 years old, I moved to Canada to study Chemical Engineering at one of the top Engineering universities in the world - University of Waterloo. I participated in chemistry olympiads and conferences when I was in high school and wanted to continue studying a subject related to chemistry. 

Couple of years into my degree, I was looking for a career transition and decided to learn how to code. I started with Codecademy and Codecademy and online education completely changed my life. 

This video is not even sponsored by them (I wish it was, hey Codecademy, pls, sponsor me!) but I am a huge believer in the platform. I quickly got hooked on coding because of how interactive the web development course on Codecademy was (I took the html, css class) and then I transitioned to taking more coding courses on Coursera (another favorite of mine). I’m also going to leave a link to the video where I talk about the best online platforms to learn coding. 

Fast forward, 6 months into learning, I moved to San Francisco for the first time to intern at Yelp, which kickstarted my career in tech. I quickly fell in love with the industry and Silicon Valley - I was constantly surrounded by really smart people who were bursting with ideas, as an immigrant from Eastern Europe, I always wanted to live in a vibrant city, and San Francisco was perfect. I felt like I was learning and growing like never before. 

I then had an opportunity to work on the biggest Canadian hackathon (Hack the North), went on to work as an Engineer at Airbnb, started a collaborative fraud organization Risksalon.org along with an annual conference, most importantly I started this YouTube channel and this awesome community! 

Learning how to code has allowed me the freedom to reflect on my choices, to reflect on what is it that I’m excited about, and incredible opportunities to work on impactful projects and freedom to think about what’s next. Since about a year ago, after reflecting on what I wanted to do, I transitioned into first a Chief of Staff role, then into a Product Manager role, all within Airbnb. I’ve now been living in Silicon Valley for a few years and who knows where life will take me next :)  

I want you to take a few things away from this video: 

1. Tech is full of opportunities and my own journey is great example of this 
2. Frequently spend time reflecting on your life and your choices: are you excited about what you are doing, what is your north start, are you doing the right things to move into that direction. 
3. If you want to pick up any new skill, all you have to do is to put your mind to it and put in the work - I am a strong believer that you can learn anything, especially nowadays, when we have access to such incredible cluster of online learning
4. Take good care of yourself - you are your biggest asset and you need to make sure that you give this asset enough energy to keep going, to keep dreaming, and to keep executing 

#Motivation #TechTips

snippet.title: How to stay productive when working in remote teams
snippet.description:
Book a 1:1 call with me - https://www.superpeer.com/luba

The world is becoming more and more distributed, so knowing how to work remotely is of utmost importance these days. I work at Airbnb in Silicon Valley and my company developed a great list with guidelines on how to be successful remote. I also have an exciting announcement coming at the end of the video, so make sure you stick around!

Overcommunicate 
It’s easy to fall into a rut of not talking to colleagues directly when you aren’t in direct, interpersonal contact everyday. Make an effort to check in with your teammates, jump on a video or a phone call with them. People want to stay connected and it’s always better to do it live than through digital back and forth. 

You might want to establish a cadence of daily virtual team standup to ensure consistency of execution. 

When communicating with others remotely, always assume a positive intent and lean into partnership. 

Working blocks and Time Zones
One of the challenges of working remotely can be that people are in different time zones and on different time scheduled. Make sure that your team knows your work hours and the timezone you are in: you can add both in Google Calendar, it will also automatically gray out the times when you are not working. Overall, set very clear expectations about your schedule with others. If you’re using a tool like Slack, you can include your time zone in it and it will automatically show people what time it’s for you if it’s in a different timezone. 

Running virtual meetings
There’s plenty of tools to run virtual meetings nowadays, but by far my favorite is Zoom. It’s very reliable, fast, and easy to use. When running a virtual meeting, ask everyone to turn their camera on: I know it might be uncomfortable at first, but it can ensure that you stay connected with your team. If you are using Zoom, use Gallery view as it encourages full participation and attention from all members. When you are in meetings though, make sure to mute your mic when you are not speaking and sit in a quiet environment when you do :) 

Brainstorming

Since we don’t have a shared physical space, many people struggle with the need of a virtual device that allows for fruitful collaboration. I can suggest a few tools: Jamboard is great for white boarding, Miro is great for post it brainstorms. 

I also have a cool announcement, you can now book time for 1:1 calls with me on Superpeer (https://www.superpeer.com/luba) a platform that a friend of mine recently launched!

snippet.title: Top 5 Careers In Tech 2020
snippet.description:
Check out Classpert, search engine for online courses: https://clas.pt/classpert_

Tech has a variety of opportunities and not just software engineer. You don't have to learn to code to transition into tech and in this video I am going over the top careers in tech with no requirement to be technical (to code). 

1. Product Manager. Product Manager is a great role for someone who wants to oversee product strategy, team roadmap, goals, and vision. You will be working cross functional partners such as designers, data scientists, content managers who will execute on the product you are building. 

2. Content Strategist. If you love language and storytelling, content strategist might be a role for you. Any text you see on Facebook, Airbnb, Google, is created by a content strategist. They are ensuring that the use of words represents the values of the brand and the message is consistent across the platform. 

3. Technical Program Manager. TPM is an enabler for better processes and visibility across the companies, they help the teams to execute more efficiently. TPMs leverage your expertise to identify and define the most critical priorities and establish best practices for the team.

4. UX Designer. If you’re good at identifying and articulating the strengths and weaknesses of products, understanding user needs, and sifting through data, UX design could be calling your name. Plus, you’ll have the satisfaction of making your users’ lives easier, and creating the product designs. 

5. Chief of Staff. Super hot and growing role right now, you can be working directly with the CEO or another leader at the company. You are leader's right hand and strategic partner for the leader you're working with, so you will have an opportunity to work on a variety of initiatives.

snippet.title: How To Stay Productive When Working At Home (tips from a tech worker)
snippet.description:
I’ve been working from home for a bit over a week now due to the quarantine. As a tech area in Silicon Valley, we do get a chance to work from home once a week, but doing so all the time is different. Here are my tips for how to work from home as a tech employee (or any other employee) but still be productive: 

1. Make the bed in the morning. Great way to start your day feeling accomplished and ready for more accomplishments in the day. 
2. Get dressed as if you’re going into the office - shower, put your favorite outfit on, makeup If you were it. This will help you feel good and feel prepared for a great day ahead of you. 
3. Find a dedicated workspace in your home - DO NOT work from your bed. Find a desk, buy a desk, make sure that you know that this space is for doing work. 
4. Interact with people - make sure to avoid feeling lonely, call your friends and family. 
5. Pomodoro technique for staying focused - 25 mins on, 5 mins off. Don’t forget to take breaks. 
6. Make a todo list of all the things you’re hoping to accomplish in the day. Having a plan will keep you grounded and it will feel great checking items off your list throughout the day. 

I hope you find these tips actionable and useful!

snippet.title: How To Start A Career In Tech In 2020 // Ultimate Skill
snippet.description:
Breaking into a new industry, or into a new role can be very challenging - it’s competitive out there, it’s hard to figure out how to make your skills transferrable, and it can be overwhelming. 

In this video today, I will tell you about the number one thing that will help you get started with your career in tech. This strategy will allow you get an idea for how to prepare for interviews and ultimately get these initial interviews. 

Networking, and relationship building is extremely important when starting a new career. When I decided to transition from chemical engineering to software engineering, networking allowed me to get my first coding internship. 

1. It is of utmost importance to keep up with your old connections from all walks of live. Referrals at tech companies are everything: every day recruiters at big tech companies receive thousands of job applications, I, as a Product Manager at Airbnb receive multiple messages a week from a friend asking to refer someone to a job at Airbnb. You want to make sure you keep up those close connections to be able to ask for a referral. 

2. Don’t be afraid to reach out to people you don’t know. Ask them for 20 minutes of their time and buy them a coffee. You’d be surprised how much people are willing to give you their advise, time, and offer help. At the end of this conversation, ask them to introduce you to 2 more people you should meet. 

3. Go to events: there’s plenty of networking events, hackathons, meetups in every city. Get out of your comfort zone, meet new people, and don’t forget to offer them help.
